exercise2.prompt: Import random, list its contents with dir(), and read the documentation for choice()

exercise2.hint: dir() answers "what is in here" and help() answers "what does this one do". The exercise asks both questions, so it needs both calls.

choices: Copies the math module's code into your file
Loads the module and binds the name math to it
Makes sqrt available as a bare name
questions.explain: The import runs the module once and gives you one name for it. Everything inside stays behind that name, which is why it is math.sqrt and not sqrt.
The import statement brings the module in, and the module prefix says where randint came from.

questions.prompt: Match each module to the kind of work it is for.
questions.explain: Each module gathers one area of work. Knowing which module owns a job is most of knowing where to look for the function.

questions.prompt: Which of these are reasons to split code into modules?
choices: The same function can be reused by several programs
A fix made in one place reaches everything that imports it
Two modules can each have a function called load without clashing
Code inside a module runs faster than code in the main file
questions.explain: Reuse, one place to fix, and separate namespaces are all real. Speed is not: a module is the same code, just kept somewhere else.
